question: A 50-year-old woman with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) presents to your clinic with complaints of left eye pain and reduced vision. She notes that she was in her usual state of health until 3 days prior to presentation when she noticed some mild tenderness around her left eye, unrelieved by any pain relievers. This morning when she woke up she was unable to see out of her left eye and made an appointment to come see you. Other than SLE, her medical history is unremarkable. She has had no additional symptoms other than pain and vision loss. Her vital signs are all within normal limits. On exam, she has no vision in her left eye, but 20/30 visual acuity in her right eye. When you shine a light in her left eye there is no response. What response would you expect when you shine a light in her right eye?

options.B: Miosis of the right eye only
options.C: Miosis of the left eye only

The acute onset of pain and vision loss in one eye, with no response to light, suggests a possible inflammatory process affecting the eye. Given the patient's history of SLE, the most likely diagnosis is scleritis. Scleritis is an inflammation of the sclera, the white part of the eye.

Scleritis can be associated with systemic autoimmune diseases like SLE. The inflammation can cause pain, redness, and vision loss. The lack of response to light indicates a problem with the optic nerve or retina, which is consistent with scleritis.

In scleritis, the inflammation can affect the ciliary body, which is responsible for accommodation (focusing). This can lead to a decreased ability to focus, which can manifest as blurred vision or difficulty seeing close objects.

The question asks what response we would expect when shining a light in the right eye. Since the patient has no other symptoms, and the left eye is affected, the right eye should be normal. Therefore, we would expect a normal pupillary response to light.
